provenance: Reviewed snapshot of Nivesh learning notes; original educational prose, source links are further reading.

foundations.title: 1. Start with the business
foundations.note: A stock represents an ownership interest. Before forecasting its price, explain who pays the company, what they buy and why they return. Sketch inputs → operations → customers. A sector name is only a starting label; businesses within it can have different economics.
foundations.task: Pick two understandable sectors. Write one measurable demand question for each; favour the one whose customers and evidence you can explain.
foundations.question: Which is the best starting research question?
options: Who buys this product, and what changes their spending?
foundations.explanation: Customer economics gives you a testable business question; a desired return or popularity does not.

foundations.title: 2. Choose companies and collect evidence
foundations.note: Compare two or three companies with similar products and geography. Confirm legal names, symbols, dates and reporting basis. Use filings for disclosed facts; label management guidance, outside estimates and your assumptions separately. Missing evidence is a research task.
foundations.task: Open the screener, shortlist two peers, then save their original annual-report links and three unanswered questions in a company notebook.
foundations.question: A news story mentions a project bid. What is established?
options: A reported bid needs checking against an original disclosure
foundations.explanation: Bid, award, execution, recognised revenue and collected cash are different stages.

foundations.title: 3. Read the accounts together
foundations.note: The balance sheet is a dated snapshot; income and cash-flow statements cover periods. Profit and operating cash can diverge. Read notes and auditor commentary, then compare the same consolidated or standalone basis and units.
foundations.task: For two years, record revenue, profit, operating cash, debt and receivables with page references. Explain one change using the notes.
foundations.question: Profit rose but receivables grew much faster. What next?
options: Inspect collection, revenue recognition and cash flow
foundations.explanation: This is a reason to investigate cash conversion, not proof of misconduct.

foundations.title: 4. Build a demand and supply model
foundations.note: Build revenue from operating drivers: units × realised price, or customers × spending. Check capacity, utilisation, competition and substitutes. A growing market does not guarantee company growth. Avoid counting both market share gains and the same volume gains twice.
foundations.task: Choose one company; write three drivers, their sources and the evidence that would contradict each. Banks and insurers need specialised models.
foundations.question: An industry adds substantial capacity. What should you test?
foundations.explanation: Supply can grow faster than demand, putting pressure on prices and returns.

foundations.title: 5. Turn news into research questions
foundations.note: Use event → actual company exposure → operating change → financial effect → timing. Check the original release, effective date and counterarguments. A policy proposal, funding allocation and paid order are different evidence. Good business news can already be reflected in the price.
foundations.task: Read one India and one world headline. Record who benefits, who pays, what must happen first and what evidence would prove you wrong.
foundations.question: Oil falls. Does every cement company benefit equally?
options: No; check fuel mix, contracts, freight and selling prices
foundations.explanation: Exposure and pass-through determine the business effect; expectations also affect stock prices.

foundations.title: 6. Separate a good company from its price
foundations.note: Valuation asks what assumptions a price requires. Compare bear, base and bull operating cases. For profitable non-financial firms, a simplified EPS × assumed P/E exercise can reveal sensitivity. Losses, cyclicals, banks and insurers require different treatment.
foundations.task: Use the practice lab. Raise profit but lower the assumed multiple; explain how a stronger business can still produce a lower price scenario.
foundations.question: EPS rises 10%, while P/E falls 20%. What happens to EPS × P/E?
foundations.explanation: 1.10 × 0.80 = 0.88. A multiple change can outweigh earnings growth.

foundations.title: 7. Think about losses and portfolios
foundations.note: Risk includes permanent loss, funding pressure, concentration and being forced to sell. Match investments to horizon and liquidity needs. Diversification reduces some concentration risk, but does not eliminate losses. Several funds can still hold overlapping exposures.
foundations.task: List three ways your thesis fails. Check whether your other ideas depend on the same rate, commodity or customer cycle.
foundations.question: Five stocks all depend on the same commodity. Are you broadly diversified?
options: No, their business risks may overlap
foundations.explanation: Count underlying exposures, not just tickers.

foundations.title: 8. Compare strategies honestly
foundations.note: A strategy needs explicit selection, sizing, entry, exit and review rules. Test costs, liquidity, benchmark choice and unseen periods. A backtest can accidentally use future information or omit failed companies. A convincing historical chart is not a promise.
foundations.task: Compare two strategy cards. Write the environment where each could fail, then inspect the assumptions in the backtester before running an example.
foundations.question: A test uses today's index members for ten years of history. What is a concern?
options: No issue if returns look strong
foundations.explanation: Today's members exclude some firms that failed or left; results can be distorted.

foundations.title: 9. Write and challenge a stock pitch
foundations.note: Present a business, a differentiated thesis, evidence, scenarios, catalysts and failure conditions. Separate fact from interpretation. Show what expectations you disagree with and why. Keep a dated record and compare later results with your original assumptions.
foundations.task: Use the pitch worksheet. Ask a club member to argue the opposite case. A watch or insufficient-evidence conclusion is valid.
foundations.question: Which thesis is most testable?
options: Collections improve by next results; track receivable days and CFO
foundations.explanation: A measurable outcome and review date make it possible to revise a view honestly.

strategies.name: Value
strategies.idea: Pay less than a justified estimate of business value.
strategies.evidence: Normalised earnings, assets, cash generation and valuation scenarios.
strategies.failure: A cheap business can deteriorate; a catalyst may never arrive.
strategies.task: Explain why a low multiple is deserved or mistaken.

strategies.name: Growth
strategies.idea: Study durable expansion and reinvestment opportunities.
strategies.evidence: Customer demand, unit economics, competitive supply and financing.
strategies.failure: Overpaying or disappointing growth can overwhelm business progress.
strategies.task: Separate market growth from company share gains.

strategies.name: Quality
strategies.idea: Seek resilient profitability and financial strength.
strategies.evidence: Cash conversion, leverage, repeat demand and capital allocation.
strategies.failure: Quality can be overpriced or weaken as competition changes.
strategies.task: Challenge one apparently strong metric using the accounts.

strategies.name: Momentum
strategies.idea: Use explicit rules based on past relative price strength.
strategies.evidence: Adjusted prices, turnover, liquidity and realistic transaction costs.
strategies.failure: Sharp reversals, crowding and trading costs.
strategies.task: Specify formation period, rebalancing and exit rules before testing.

strategies.name: Broad index investing
strategies.idea: Follow a defined broad market index.
strategies.evidence: Index coverage, concentration, fees and tracking difference.
strategies.failure: Market losses remain; a sector index can be concentrated.
strategies.task: Read an index methodology and a fund factsheet.

strategies.name: Event-driven research
strategies.idea: Investigate a specific change such as capacity, a policy or an award.
strategies.evidence: Original disclosures, conditions, timing and cash consequences.
strategies.failure: The event can fail, be delayed or already be priced in.
strategies.task: Track bid → award → execution → collection separately.
